title: Private connectivity discovery - MapleWorks
meeting_header: Date: 2025-06-12 | Start: 16:00 UTC | Duration: 47m | Attendees: Carlos Vega (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jamie Lin (MapleWorks - Infra), Arun Rao (MapleWorks - Security), Melissa Chu (MapleWorks - Platform)
summary: Discovery focused on Private/VPC connectivity for Redwood Private: VPC peering vs PrivateLink, CIDR and routing constraints, cross-account peering, egress controls, region availability, and security/compliance requirements. Customer wants a pilot in us-east-1 and eu-west-1 with strict egress controls and KMS integration. Action: send network worksheet, share SOC2/KMS docs, schedule hands-on peering test.
topics: CIDR overlap and transit VPC patterns
action_items: Carlos Vega: Send MapleWorks VPC network worksheet and sample CloudFormation peering template; due 2025-06-16
Priya Nair: Prepare checklist for Private endpoints and suggested security controls (IAM roles, VPC endpoints, SGs); due 2025-06-18
MapleWorks (Jamie): Share current VPC CIDR ranges and account IDs for peering test; due 2025-06-15
next_steps: Redwood to share network worksheet and SOC2 + KMS/HSM docs
Schedule 1-hour hands-on peering test in staging (us-east-1)
MapleWorks to provide VPC CIDR and AWS account IDs
Redwood to scope pilot pricing for Dedicated Private deployment
transcript:
00:00:00 - Meeting started
00:00:03 - Carlos (Redwood AE): Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
00:00:10 - Jamie (MapleWorks): Jamie here. Hi.
00:00:12 - Arun (MapleWorks): Arun, hi.
00:00:14 - Melissa (MapleWorks): Melissa here.
00:00:16 - Priya (Redwood SE): Priya joining from the SE side. Thanks for the time.
00:00:20 - Carlos: Great. Goal for today — understand your networking constraints for Redwood Private and map out a pilot. We'll talk peering, private endpoints, regions, and security controls.
00:00:34 - Jamie: Yeah, high level we want to run models behind our VPC. Low latency is a must, we also need to ensure data never leaves our accounts, and egress is tightly controlled. We're leaning toward a private deployment, but we're still evaluating dedicated vs private, and whether PrivateLink is better than peering.
00:00:52 - Priya: Totally. We usually cover three patterns: VPC peering (cross-account), AWS PrivateLink (interface endpoints), and transit/VPN patterns for on-prem. Each has tradeoffs — peering supports full-routed traffic but CIDR can't overlap, private link gives you per-service endpoints and avoids routing changes.
00:01:12 - Arun: On CIDR, we have overlapping ranges across some of our older accounts, that's a big blocker for peering unless we use NAT or intermediate transit.
00:01:20 - Carlos: Yeah. Do you have a sense of the accounts and whether you can resize or use secondary ranges?
00:01:26 - Jamie: We can provide ranges; resizing takes weeks because of dependent infra. We prefer not to re-IP if possible.
00:01:33 - Priya: Understood. For overlapping CIDR, one option is Transit Gateway with route table translation or using a Proxy pattern — Redwood can expose a PrivateLink endpoint into your VPC which avoids peering and CIDR constraints. It also gives a bit more control on allowed principals.
00:01:49 - Melissa: Can you clarify the PrivateLink approach? Is that something Redwood hosts in our account or you create endpoints in our VPC?
00:01:58 - Priya: Good question. For AWS, Redwood can publish a service in our account and you create an interface endpoint in your VPC that points to us. There are two deployment flavors: 1) Redwood-managed service (we provision the service) and you create an endpoint — standard PrivateLink; 2) For Redwood Private (customer-managed control plane), we deploy in your VPC or account and you run the service locally. In the latter case, peering or direct VPC attachments apply.
00:02:21 - Arun: Does the PrivateLink path still route tokens via public internet or is it fully private? We need to ensure traffic doesn't egress via internet gateways.
00:02:30 - Priya: Interface endpoints are ENIs in your subnet so traffic to the service stays on the AWS network — it's private. There is some AWS-managed ENI traffic, but it doesn't traverse the public internet.
00:02:41 - Jamie: Ok. On regions: we need us-east-1 and eu-west-1. Does Redwood Private support multi-region deployments?
00:02:49 - Carlos: Yes, you can deploy Private in multiple regions. You'll need per-region VPCs and either cross-region peering or a replication/failover plan. For strict data residency we can pin models to region.
00:03:02 - Melissa: Is cross-region peering different? Any gotchas?
00:03:06 - Priya: Cross-region peering is supported but latency and egress costs matter. For active-active multi-region, we recommend running Redwood nodes in both regions and a DNS-based routing or smart routing to keep latency minimal.
00:03:18 - Arun: On KMS — we need CMKs in our account. Can Redwood integrate with our KMS for model keys or token encryption?
00:03:27 - Carlos: Yes, Redwood supports customer-managed KMS keys for data at rest encryption and for secrets via KMS integration. For keys used by Redwood components, we usually set up cross-account IAM roles with key usage permissions; Priya can outline exact IAM trust policy and rotation.
00:03:42 - Priya: We'll send example IAM policy snippets. Quick note: if you want HSM-level isolation, we support HSM-backed keys if you supply the key material. We'll include our compliance docs.
00:03:52 - Jamie: Great. We also need audit logs forwarded to our SIEM. How granular are your logs?
00:03:58 - Carlos: The Redwood Console can stream audit logs (API calls, model metadata) to S3 or to a logging endpoint. We can also forward CloudWatch logs (for AWS) — many customers push them to Sumo or Splunk. We'll include the schemas.
00:04:12 - Arun: Any concerns with PII or model caching? We have strict retention policies and would like KV cache disabled.
00:04:20 - Priya: By default we have prefix caching and KV cache as optimizations; in private deployments we can disable KV caching or configure TTLs. We'll show how to set cache policies per-model/route.
00:04:33 - Jamie: Good. Back to peering — one of our constraints is that some teams are in a different AWS org. Cross-account peering is OK, but we need to avoid giving broad routing. Is it possible to peer only to specific subnets?
00:04:47 - Priya: VPC peering is at the VPC level, you control which subnets can talk via security groups and route tables. For more surgical access, PrivateLink is preferred because it uses interface endpoints in specific subnets and security groups to limit scope.
00:05:01 - Melissa: Do you have examples of the security group rules we should use for PrivateLink endpoints?
00:05:06 - Priya: Yes — typical SG allows outbound to the PrivateLink ENI on port 443 from the app subnets and inbound from the ENI. We'll send a snippet.
00:05:15 - Jamie: About DNS resolution — if we create an interface endpoint, do we need to manage private hosted zones? We have split-horizon DNS.
00:05:23 - Priya: AWS provides private DNS for endpoints but if you have split-horizon you'll want to control the records in Route53 private zones. We can support either; sometimes customers prefer to override the A records to force endpoint resolution.
00:05:35 - Arun: What's the expected maintenance window for Redwood Private? Patching, upgrades — do you coordinate?
00:05:41 - Carlos: For Private deployments we coordinate maintenance windows with the customer; we provide versioned rollouts and can do canary updates. SLA depends on the reserved capacity and support tier.
00:05:50 - Jamie: On IP addressing — our security team wants to limit egress to a set of NAT IPs. If the service runs in your account, can we lock down traffic to those egress IPs?
:00:06:00 - Priya: If you use PrivateLink, traffic stays within AWS and the destination is service-managed; however, the ENIs have AWS-owned IPs in your subnets. For Redwood-managed hosted endpoints, we can publish a set of egress IP ranges for firewall allowlisting. For dedicated private deployments in your VPC, you control NAT and egress IPs directly.
00:06:24 - Melissa: You mentioned RBAC earlier — can you integrate with our SSO (SAML/Okta)? We need role-based access and audit trails.
00:06:32 - Carlos: Yes, Redwood Console supports SAML SSO with SCIM for provisioning and RBAC roles. We'll include our SSO integration guide.
00:06:41 - Arun: Any requirement for network ACLs or can we just use SGs? Our security standard requires NACLs at the subnet level for egress controls.
00:06:49 - Priya: NACLs are fine — just be careful with ephemeral ENIs for PrivateLink. Ensure the NACL allows the ephemeral port ranges and TCP 443. We'll add an example.
00:06:59 - Jamie: How does billing work for Private vs Dedicated vs Hosted? We need to present CAPEX vs OPEX to finance.
00:07:07 - Carlos: Hosted is pay-as-you-go per-token; Dedicated is a reserved capacity SKU with monthly commits; Private (customer-managed) has platform licensing plus infra costs — we can put together a comparative TCO for your workload. For pilot pricing we'll propose a small Dedicated commitment or a timebound Private pilot.
00:07:27 - Melissa: We want predictable latency. Can you give numbers for cold start token latency in Private deployments?
00:07:34 - Priya: Rough guidance — in-region Private deployments we see tail latencies under 100ms per token for smaller models and 150–300ms for larger family under steady-state; of course kernel selection, batching, and sequence lengths affect that. We'll include benchmark slides.
00:07:50 - Arun: On compliance, we need SOC2 Type II evidence, data flow diagrams, and penetration test reports.
00:07:57 - Carlos: We'll share SOC2, penetration test summaries, and architecture diagrams. For data flow we'll diagram how requests move from your VPC to model nodes and where logs land.
00:08:08 - Jamie: Ok, let's walk through a concrete pilot: goal is to validate connectivity and latency for our chat assistant. We want to test in us-east-1 using an interface endpoint first. Step one we provide account IDs and CIDRs; step two Redwood provides QuickStart templates or CFN; step three we run a small perf test. Timeline target: two weeks. Is that reasonable?
00:08:28 - Carlos: Two weeks for the initial connectivity and perf sanity is reasonable if you can provide account info and a contact for the cloud infra team.
00:08:36 - Jamie: I'll be the point for infra. We'll gather account IDs.
00:08:39 - Melissa: Who from Redwood will be hands-on during the peering test?
00:08:43 - Carlos: Priya will take lead on the technical test, I'll coordinate and attach a solutions engineer if needed.
00:08:48 - Priya: Yep — we'll do a runbook and a Zoom pairing session for the test.
00:08:53 - Arun: A quick question — how do you handle secrets (API keys) inside our VPC?
00:08:59 - Priya: Secrets can be stored in Vault or AWS Secrets Manager in your account; Redwood supports retrieving via cross-account IAM roles or you can push secrets during initial bootstrap. For maximum control, customers keep secrets in their own KMS and we never persist them in plaintext.
00:09:14 - Jamie: We also need egress logging to be tamper-evident. Can logs be SHA-summed and shipped to our secure S3?
00:09:21 - Carlos: We can stream logs to your S3 and you can enable object lock or use KMS and fine-grained permissions for tamper protection. We'll provide a recommended config.
00:09:33 - Melissa: Anything special for Azure or GCP? We run some workloads in GCP but primary is AWS.
00:09:39 - Priya: For GCP we have equivalents — Private Service Connect for private endpoints, and VPC peering. Patterns are similar but implementation details differ. We'll include a short cross-cloud note.
00:09:50 - Jamie: Competitors — have you seen customers use Anthropic or OpenAI with a similar private connectivity pattern?
00:09:57 - Carlos: Yes; Anthropic and OpenAI generally offer hosted private connectivity via enterprise agreements, but the difference is around control and deploy options. Redwood emphasizes private deployments and dedicated capacity with more control over caching and kernel selection.
00:10:11 - Arun: Any known limitations with PrivateLink and high-throughput workloads?
00:10:16 - Priya: PrivateLink scales but ENI and endpoint throughput can hit soft limits; we recommend testing throughput patterns. For very high QPS, peering with dedicated nodes in your VPC or Dedicated reserved capacity is a better fit.
00:10:30 - Jamie: Ok — let's capture the immediate asks.
00:10:33 - Carlos: Action items recap — we'll send the network worksheet, SOC2 and KMS docs, and a CFN snippet. Maples (Jamie) will provide account IDs and CIDRs. We'll schedule the peering test next week.
00:10:45 - Melissa: Sounds good.
00:10:47 - Arun: Quick nit — do you support mutual TLS between client and Redwood nodes? Some of our teams require mTLS.
00:10:55 - Priya: We do support mTLS in Private deployments, yes. We'll include the cert exchange process in the checklist.
00:11:03 - Jamie: Thanks. Anything else we should consider?
00:11:07 - Carlos: One more note on cost controls — Redwood Optimize can suggest batching and quantization profiles to reduce cost. In private deployments you can push quantized model variants to reduce GPU memory and latency tradeoffs.
00:11:20 - Jamie: Great. Let's stop here and follow up via email with the worksheet.
00:11:25 - Carlos: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up with docs and proposed times for the peering test.
00:11:30 - Meeting ended

Notes: Transcription contains occasional mis-heard words (Red wood, privatee endpoints). Some speaker labels may be approximate. The technical content above includes typical customer questions around CIDR overlap, Transit Gateway vs PrivateLink, KMS integration, audit logs, and pilot scoping.
